title: Events and Forms
summary: React events let a component respond to a click or a typed value. Forms group inputs together.
introduction: React events let a component respond to a click or a typed value. Forms group inputs together. Build a small form. Keep its current text in state and show what happens when the reader presses the submit button.
learningObjectives: Attach event handlers and read the event object
Build controlled inputs whose value lives in state
Handle form submission without a page reload
Use form Actions and useActionState for async submissions

blocks.text: Handlers are passed as props named after the event in camelCase: `onClick`, `onChange`, `onSubmit`, `onKeyDown`. You pass the **function itself**, not a call. React attaches one native listener at the root and dispatches to your handlers with an event object that has the same properties and methods as the DOM event: `target`, `currentTarget`, `preventDefault()`, `stopPropagation()`.

blocks.title: Toolbar.jsx
Console after clicking Save, then Delete

blocks.text: Use an inline arrow function when you need to pass arguments or the handler is a one-liner; use a named function when it has several lines. Both are fine. Handlers can also be passed down as props (`onRemove`) so a parent decides what a click means, as the [components lesson](/tutorials/react/components-props) showed.

blocks.title: Common mistake: calling the handler instead of passing it
blocks.text: `<button onClick={handleSave()}>` runs `handleSave` during rendering, not on click, and passes its return value (`undefined`) as the handler. Write `onClick={handleSave}` or `onClick={() => handleSave(id)}`. The same applies to `onSubmit` and every other event prop.

In plain HTML an input keeps its own value. In React you usually make the input **controlled**: its `value` comes from state and `onChange` writes every keystroke back into that state. The state is then the single source of truth, which makes validation, formatting and resetting trivial.

blocks.title: NameForm.jsx

blocks.text: `onChange` in React fires on every keystroke (unlike the DOM `change` event, which waits until the field loses focus). Checkboxes use `checked` and `e.target.checked` instead of `value`; `<select>` and `<textarea>` both take `value`, with no `selected` attribute on options.

A form with several fields usually keeps one object in state, updated by a single handler that uses the input's `name`. On submit you call `preventDefault()`; otherwise the browser performs a full page load with the values in the URL.

blocks.title: SignupForm.jsx
Console: ada@example.com, Pro plan and checked box submitted

blocks.text: The computed property name `[name]` lets one handler serve every field. `required` and `type="email"` give you the browser's built-in validation for free; the submit handler only runs once it passes.

Not every field needs state. If you only care about the values at submit time, leave the inputs uncontrolled and read them from the form element with `FormData`. This is less code, and it is also the model that React 19 Actions build on.

blocks.title: SearchForm.jsx
Console after typing "hooks" and pressing Enter

blocks.text: React 19 lets you pass a function to the form's `action` prop. React calls it with the `FormData`, and if the function is `async` React tracks it as an **Action**: it knows when the submission is pending, resets uncontrolled fields when it finishes, and `useActionState` exposes the result. This replaces a lot of hand-written `isSubmitting` and `error` state.

blocks.title: Subscribe.jsx
The message below the button
blocks.content:
submit "ada" →

Enter a valid email address.

submit "ada@example.com" →

Subscribed ada@example.com.

blocks.text: `useActionState(action, initialState)` returns the latest value the action returned, a wrapped action to put on the form, and a pending flag. The action receives the previous state first and the `FormData` second. For a submit button nested deep inside the form, `useFormStatus` from `react-dom` reads the same pending flag without prop drilling.

questions.question: Which pair of props makes an `<input>` controlled?
questions.explanation: A controlled input reads its `value` from state and reports every change through `onChange`. `defaultValue` is the uncontrolled alternative.

questions.question: In React, `onChange` on a text input fires only when the field loses focus.
questions.explanation: React's `onChange` fires on every keystroke, like the DOM `input` event. The DOM `change` event is the one that waits for blur.

seo.title: React Events and Forms – Controlled Inputs and Actions
seo.description: Handle events in React 19, build controlled inputs, submit forms without a reload, read FormData and use form Actions with useActionState for async submits.
